statements.statement: TTL is a cache invalidation strategy that ensures data is always fresh.
statements.explanation: TTL stands for time-to-live and only sets an expiration time on cached data. Although simple, it can lead to stale data until the expiration time is reached.

statements.statement: Explicit invalidation requires that the cache is updated every time the database changes.
statements.explanation: Explicit invalidation involves manually removing or updating cache entries when the database is modified. This ensures fresher data but requires careful management to ensure all changes are captured.

statements.statement: TTL cache invalidation is typically more complex to implement than explicit invalidation.
statements.explanation: TTL is simpler to implement as it only involves setting an expiration time for cache entries, whereas explicit invalidation requires additional mechanisms to track and update cache changes.

statements.statement: A hybrid strategy that starts with TTL and introduces explicit invalidation where needed can be effective.
statements.explanation: Starting with TTL provides a simple foundation, and explicit invalidation can be added for situations where staleness is unacceptable, balancing simplicity and freshness.
